body_markdown:
Conventional wisdom says to buy the best car you can afford. Certainly, that’s a better argument than buying the worst car you can afford. Easier said than done, however, because sometimes that’s exactly what we do.


Mark Twain once wrote that “the difference between the almost right word and the right word is really a large matter—it’s the difference between the lightning bug and the lightning.” In a way, the same can be said for much of the classic and enthusiast car market, where the difference in value between a car in #2 (excellent) condition and that same car in #4 (fair) condition can really be a large matter—if not in appearance from 10 feet, then certainly in the price you’ll pay to acquire it.


When it comes to lightning and lightning bugs, nowhere is the divide more evident than in the five cars highlighted here. For many years, none of these vehicles was viewed as collectible; when they changed hands they were simply used cars. Most individual examples of each still are just that—and are priced accordingly. Encountering a truly stand-out example is often rarer than finding an excellent vintage Ferrari, for example, because restorations are expensive and rarely make sense for many cars. So, the excellent ones you do see tend to be all original and well-kept, often from long-term ownership, and that kind of love will come with a big premium.


The cars below represent some of the biggest valuation gaps in the market, calculated as a percent comparison of fair and excellent condition. The prices shown represent average #2 and average #4 values for all trims, as listed in the latest update to the Hagerty Price Guide.


## 1984–95 Mercedes-Benz 300D: 1622%


Wikimedia Commons/Johannes Maximilian


[#2 Value—$35,150 / #4 Value—$2167](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mercedes~benz/300d/1990/1990-mercedes~benz-300d-2.5?id=aCn1I000000DFeqSAG&condition=excellent)


Few cars have been as holistically executed as the W124 Mercedes. Designed under[Bruno Sacco’s leadership](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/bruno-saccos-designs-took-mercedes-benz-to-new-heights/) , the luxury sedans (which would come to be called the E-Class in Mercedes’ new-for-’93 naming conventions) offered space, sensible but plush interiors, innovative technologies, and construction to rival the Everlasting Gobstopper. Power came from four-, five-, six-, and eight-cylinder engines, in both gas and diesel guise. While the[Porsche-built 500E](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/30-years-on-the-mercedes-benz-500-e-proves-the-power-of-partnership/) is probably the most exclusive and desirable of the range, the most durable is likely the 300D, initially powered by a 143-horsepower 3.0-liter inline-six turbodiesel and then, after 1990, by a 121-hp 2.5-liter inline-five turbodiesel.


A handful of W124 Mercedes made the list of cars with the biggest valuation gap, but the 300D topped it. These cars were known to go for several hundred thousand miles, but such distances, and the accompanying wear and tear, don’t lend themselves to creampuff status, so most examples you see today may be perfectly usable, but needy and tired. All of which makes for a low-four-digit ride. Find a pristine one, however, and expect to pay way, way up.


##
1971–73 Volvo 1800ES: 1187%


Volvo


[#2 Value—$58,200 / #4 Value—$4900](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/volvo/1800es/1972/1972-volvo-1800es-base?id=aCn1I000000DT5LSAW&condition=excellent)


Even today, it’s hard to believe that Volvo built[the 1800](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/volvo-1800-values-on-the-rise/) , given the Swedish carmaker’s catalog to that point. The PV444/544 were great cars, but no one has ever accused them of being lookers. The P1800 coupe of 1961, on the other hand, was stunning, and the shape aged gracefully over the next decade. Even today, there’s nothing else like it on the road. Incremental updates found their way into the cars during production, but the biggest change came with the 1971 introduction of the 1800ES, a two-door wagon that added great functionality to the shape.


Just shy of 8100 were built over two years, so they were rare-ish then, and they certainly are now, as most were used up in faithful service. Although mechanically stout, rust did many of them in, and restoring one can be prohibitively expensive. Which is why great ones cost so much and[merely OK ones](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/past-sales/1973-volvo-1800es/1836354004411/ba21d2e3-6a53-45c3-918e-b20df0d1b652) … don’t.


## **** 1981–90 Toyota Land Cruiser FJ60/FJ62: 1039%


Toyota


[#2 Value—$60,000 / #4 Value—$5770](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/toyota/land_cruiser/1981/1981-toyota-land_cruiser-fj60?id=aCn1I000000DKWZSA4&condition=fair&timeframe=5Y)


Since their very first iteration way back in the early 1950s, Land Cruisers have always had a well-earned reputation for their capability, durability, and longevity. When the FJ60 assumed the wagon role in the lineup from the FJ55, it did so seamlessly, and some even welcomed its rather plain lines after the controversial styling of its (unfairly maligned) “Iron Pig” predecessor. The FJ60 morphed into[the FJ62](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/toyota/land_cruiser/1988/1988-toyota-land_cruiser-fj62?id=aCn1I000000kCiTSAU&timeframe=5Y&condition=excellent) for 1988, with the key visual difference being the switch from two round headlights to four square ones, while underhood the engine evolved from the 125-hp carbureted 4.2-liter inline-six that had been in use since the early 1960s to a 155-hp fuel-injected 4.0-liter six. The early trucks came with four-speed manuals, while FJ62s were equipped exclusively with automatics; they also offered fancy stuff like power windows and locks, along with power steering.


For a time in the 2010s, FJ40 prices went stratospheric. That never happened in quite the same way with FJ60s (or any other 4×4, for that matter), although truly exceptional ones are $100K vehicles now. But how many truly exceptional ones are there, really? No, more often than not we see super-solid #3 (good) ones in the twenty-grand range, and then honest drivers with lots of miles, a bit of bubbling here and there beneath the paint, and blanket-covered seats. These are your $6000 rigs now, which are a far cry from the occasional cherry one that saw minimal use on the hobby farm upstate. Those excellent ones have been on a steady uptick in the last few years, while rougher examples continue to fall.


##
1984–90 Ford Bronco II: 862%


Mecum


[#2 Value—$18,133 / #4 Value—$2102](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/bronco_ii/1986)


As the compact SUV craze took hold in the 1980s, Ford’s answer to the Chevy S-10 Blazer, GMC S-15 Jimmy, and Jeep Cherokee XJ was the pint-sized Bronco II, which recalled the boxy, upright looks of the very first Bronco introduced in 1966. The Ranger-based Bronco II was produced for just one generation before giving way to the Explorer, and it only ever came as a two-door model with a 115-hp (and later 140-hp) V-6 and a solid front axle on 4×4 models. Trims included Eddie Bauer and XLT, in addition to base models. Their high center of gravity and driving dynamics plagued them with a tippy reputation, which was not unjustified. Still, they were capable off-roaders prized for the hardware underpinning them and a small footprint that made them nimble in tight spaces.


Not many people have prized the Bronco II as a collectible—certainly not in the way they have the original Bronco, or even subsequent generations of the full-sizer. Perhaps no vehicle on this list better exemplifies the “just a used car” ethos than the “Baby Bronc.” And yet,[we’ve seen some well-kept great ones](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/would-you-buy-this-ford-bronco-ii-survivor-for-the-price-of-a-new-bronco-sport/) on occasion, and we included them on our[2025 Bull Market list](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/bull-market-2025/#bronco2-jump) , because there was a lot of upside for nice ones. If your goal is to beat the crap out of one in the woods, you’ve got plenty to choose from, and the crossover of Ranger parts is helpful. If you’re after a great one, you may be on the hunt for a while, but you still won’t break the bank when you land it. There’s a lot to be said for that.


##
1967–73 Honda 600: 841%


Broad Arrow


**[#2 Value—$28,600 / #4 Value—$3400](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/honda/z_600/1971/1971-honda-z_600-base?id=aCn1I000000DGm7SAG)**


Once Honda had established itself as a maker of excellent little two-wheelers, the company made the leap to cars. First came the 1963 T360 trucklet, followed almost immediately by the S500 roadster and then the S600 roadster and fastback coupe. Less specialized and more people-friendly was the tiny front-wheel-drive N360 kei car, and when it came time to bring that car to other markets, Honda upped the displacement to 598cc and called it the N600. As the company’s first official car for the American market, the N600 was a two-door sedan, and it was joined by the Z600, a two-door pillarless coupe. Both were tiny, not just by American-car standards, but even by Austin Mini standards, and they paved the way for the Civic that would take over American roads in 1972.


These days, you rarely encounter a Honda 600. Of the pair, the sportier Z600 seems to have had more staying power than the N600, but even Hagerty’s 10-year plot of 600 sales shows fewer than 40 results. Slim pickings, in other words, although seven sales in the last 12 months accurately reflect the divide between excellent and fair cars:[This 1972 Z600](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1972-honda-z600-24/) “project,” whose biggest need appeared to be new brakes, sold for just $2950 in April, while[this 66,000-mile ’71](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/1971-honda-z600-6/) , which had spent part of its life on display in a dealership, brought $30,581 back in February.
